parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a non-wage factor that might influence a person's choice of occupation?
A overtime pay
B an annual bonus
C the chance of promotion
D commission on sales
parts.answer: C the chance of promotion
parts.working: Promotion prospects are a non-wage (non-monetary) benefit of a job. Overtime pay (A), bonuses (B) and commission (D) are all forms of payment, so they are wage factors.

practice.stem: In a football factory in Sialkot, one group of workers cuts the panels, another stitches them together and a third group prints the logos.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specialisation of workers (division of labour).
parts.answer: Workers concentrating on a particular task or a narrow range of tasks, with production split into separate stages.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentrating on one task / particular job. 1 mark: production broken down into stages / tasks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the factory of its workers specialising.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: workers become more skilled and faster through repetition, so productivity rises; less time is wasted moving between tasks; training is quicker and cheaper because each worker learns only one task; it is easier to use specialist machinery; output rises and average cost falls.
parts.working: For each of two advantages: 1 mark for the advantage, 1 mark for the effect on the firm (output/costs/quality).

practice.stem:
The table shows the average monthly wage of two occupations in a country.
Occupation | Average monthly wage (Rs)
Airline pilot | 960 000
Farm labourer | 40 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the pilot's average wage is than the farm labourer's.
parts.answer: 24 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why airline pilots are paid more than farm labourers.
parts.answer: Pilots need long, expensive training and rare skills, so the supply of pilots is small, whereas almost anyone can do farm labouring, so supply is large. Demand for pilots is high because each pilot produces a very valuable service (high revenue per flight) and carries great responsibility for passengers' safety.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason (training/skills, limited supply, high demand/productivity, responsibility, risk), 1 mark for linking it to the wage.

practice.stem: Nadia has been offered two jobs: one as an economist in a government ministry and one, with a 25% higher salary, at a private bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two non-wage factors that Nadia might consider when choosing between the jobs.
parts.answer: Any two of: job security; pension; working hours; holidays; promotion prospects; working conditions; location/travel time; job satisfaction; training opportunities.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two non-wage factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Nadia might choose the lower-paid government job.
parts.answer: Government jobs often offer greater job security, so she is less likely to become unemployed; they may provide better pensions and fringe benefits; shorter or more regular working hours give a better work–life balance; she may value serving the public; together these benefits may outweigh the higher salary at the bank.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant non-wage benefit explained (max 3), 1 mark for the idea that total benefits/net advantages outweigh the higher wage.

practice.stem: A factory worker in Faisalabad is paid Rs 400 an hour for a basic week of 40 hours. Any extra hours are paid at time-and-a-half (1.5 times the basic rate). In one week he works 48 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate his gross earnings for the week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the employer pays a higher rate for overtime hours.
parts.answer: Workers value their leisure time more after a long working day, so a higher rate is needed to persuade them to work extra hours; it is cheaper for the firm than hiring and training extra workers for a short period.
parts.working: 1 mark: incentive to give up leisure / compensate for longer hours. 1 mark: cheaper or more flexible than recruiting more workers.

practice.stem: A government raises the national minimum wage by 20%. Many workers in shops, restaurants and small factories are paid at the minimum wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a national minimum wage.
parts.answer: The lowest wage rate per hour (or per month) that employers are legally allowed to pay workers, set by the government.
parts.working: 1 mark: lowest wage that can be paid. 1 mark: set by law/government.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not raising the minimum wage benefits low-paid workers.
parts.answer: Benefits those who keep their jobs, but may cost some jobs.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'benefits': higher income for those employed; reduces poverty and inequality; may motivate workers and raise productivity; encourages people into work. Up to 3 marks for 'may not': higher labour costs may make firms employ fewer workers, raising unemployment among the low-skilled; firms may replace workers with machines; prices may rise, reducing real gains; firms may cut hours or move into the informal sector, where the law is not enforced. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. depends on the size of the rise and the elasticity of demand for labour).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car manufacturer in Japan merges with a car manufacturer in Germany. What type of merger is this?
A conglomerate merger
B horizontal merger
C vertical backward merger
D vertical forward merger
parts.answer: B horizontal merger
parts.working: A horizontal merger joins two firms at the same stage of production in the same industry, as here (two car makers); the countries do not matter. A vertical merger (C, D) joins firms at different stages, e.g. a car maker and a tyre supplier; a conglomerate merger (A) joins firms in unrelated industries.

practice.stem: A rice mill in Punjab buys a chain of grocery shops that sells rice and other food to consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of merger.
parts.answer: Vertical forward merger
parts.working: B1: vertical forward (the mill moves towards the consumer, the next stage of production).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to the rice mill of this merger.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: guaranteed outlets for its rice, so it can plan production; it gains the retail profit margin that the shops used to earn; it can control how its rice is displayed and priced; it can prevent rival mills selling through the shops; it receives direct information about consumer demand.
parts.working: For each of two benefits: 1 mark for the benefit, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: A dairy company in Punjab closes several small milk-processing units and builds one large, highly automated plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define economies of scale.
parts.answer: The fall in average (unit) cost of production that occurs as a firm increases its scale of production / grows larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in average cost. 1 mark: as the firm increases its scale/size of output (long run).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two internal economies of scale that the company might gain.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: technical – large automated machines produce much more output per worker, lowering cost per litre; purchasing (bulk-buying) – buying milk, packaging and fuel in large quantities gets discounts; financial – a large firm can borrow more cheaply from banks; marketing – advertising costs are spread over more output; managerial – specialist managers can be employed.
parts.working: For each of two economies: 1 mark for naming/identifying it, 1 mark for explaining why average cost falls.

practice.stem: A dairy company expands its milk-processing plant. Before expanding, the plant produced 10 000 litres a day at a total cost of Rs 1 500 000. After expanding, it produces 40 000 litres a day at a total cost of Rs 4 800 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per litre before and after the expansion.
parts.answer: Before Rs 150 per litre; after Rs 120 per litre

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one diseconomy of scale that might occur if the company grows much larger.
parts.answer: e.g. communication problems: with many layers of management, messages are slow or distorted, decisions are delayed and mistakes are made, so average cost rises. Also: poor motivation of workers who feel unimportant; difficulty coordinating/controlling a very large firm.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a diseconomy. 1 mark: explains why it raises average cost.

practice.stem: In many towns, small family-run shops and workshops operate alongside large supermarket chains and manufacturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a firm might choose to stay small.
parts.answer: Any two of: the owner wants to keep control; the owner wants to avoid risk or extra work; the market is small or local; the product is a personal/specialised service; lack of finance for expansion; to avoid diseconomies of scale.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not small firms can survive in competition with large firms.
parts.answer: Many can survive, especially in niche or local markets, but they face disadvantages.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'can survive': offer personal service and flexibility; serve small or niche markets that large firms ignore; located close to customers; can give credit to regular customers; can respond quickly to changes; may supply large firms (subcontracting); government support schemes. Up to 3 marks for 'cannot': higher average costs because they lack economies of scale, so higher prices; harder and more costly to raise finance; cannot afford advertising or research; large firms may cut prices to drive them out. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a characteristic of a monopoly?
A many small sellers of the same product
B a single seller protected by barriers to entry
C firms that have no control over the price they charge
D easy entry of new firms into the market
parts.answer: B a single seller protected by barriers to entry
parts.working: A monopoly is a single seller (dominating the market) with barriers that stop new firms entering. Many sellers (A), no control over price (C) and free entry (D) are features of a highly competitive market.

practice.stem: At a large fruit and vegetable market (sabzi mandi) in Lahore, hundreds of traders sell very similar tomatoes, onions and potatoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a competitive market.
parts.answer: A market in which there are many firms competing to sell similar products, so no single firm can control the price.
parts.working: 1 mark: many buyers and sellers / firms competing. 1 mark: no single firm controls the price / similar products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two characteristics of a highly competitive market shown in the information.
parts.answer: Many sellers (hundreds of traders); similar (identical) products. (Also accept: price takers; easy entry.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two characteristics, ideally linked to the information.

practice.stem: A single company supplies all the electricity to the homes and businesses in a city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two barriers to entry that could stop new firms supplying electricity in the city.
parts.answer: Any two of: very high start-up costs (power stations, cables); economies of scale enjoyed by the existing firm; legal barriers such as a government licence; control of the distribution network.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two barriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of this monopoly for consumers.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: higher prices, because consumers have no alternative supplier; poor quality of service such as power cuts, because there is little pressure to improve; less choice; the firm may be inefficient, so costs and prices are higher; little incentive to innovate.
parts.working: For each of two disadvantages: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for explaining why it arises from monopoly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a monopoly can charge a higher price than a firm in a highly competitive market.
parts.answer: Consumers have no close substitutes and rivals cannot enter the market, so the monopoly can raise price without losing all its customers; a competitive firm that raised its price would lose customers to rivals.
parts.working: 1 mark: no close substitutes / barriers to entry. 1 mark: so demand does not fall to zero / it is a price maker, unlike a competitive firm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a monopoly is always worse for consumers than a competitive market.
parts.answer: Not always: economies of scale and research can benefit consumers, but higher prices and less choice are common.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'worse': higher prices and lower output; less choice; less incentive to be efficient or improve quality; high profits at consumers' expense. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': economies of scale may mean lower costs and prices; high profits can fund research and new products; avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly, e.g. water pipes); can be regulated or state-owned to protect consumers. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a measure of labour productivity?
A the total output of a firm
B output per worker per hour
C total wages paid divided by the number of workers
D the number of workers divided by total output
parts.answer: B output per worker per hour
parts.working: Labour productivity is output per worker (or per worker-hour). Total output (A) is production, not productivity – a common confusion; C is the average wage; D is the inverse of productivity (workers per unit of output).

practice.stem: Hand-knotted carpets made in Pakistan are produced mainly by workers using simple looms, while carpets in some other countries are made on large automated machines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production.
parts.answer: Labour-intensive production uses a high proportion of labour relative to capital; capital-intensive production uses a high proportion of capital (machinery) relative to labour.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour-intensive = more labour than capital. 1 mark: capital-intensive = more machinery/capital than labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why hand-knotted carpet production remains labour-intensive.
parts.answer: Labour is relatively cheap compared with expensive machinery; consumers pay a high price for hand-made quality and designs that machines cannot copy; production is in small workshops that cannot afford or finance machinery; skilled weavers are available.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem:
The table shows information about a textile mill in Faisalabad.
Year | Number of workers | Weekly output (metres of cloth)
2025 | 200 | 50 000
2026 | 180 | 54 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity (metres per worker per week) in each year.
parts.answer: 2025: 250 metres; 2026: 300 metres

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in labour productivity between 2025 and 2026.
parts.answer: +20% (increase)
parts.working: (300 − 250) ÷ 250 × 100 = 20% increase (B1, own figures from (a)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the mill may have increased labour productivity.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: training workers so they work faster and make fewer mistakes; installing more modern machinery; better organisation or division of labour; incentives such as bonuses linked to output; better working conditions that improve motivation.
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for explaining how it raises output per worker.

practice.stem: A biscuit manufacturer is deciding whether to replace 60 packing workers with automated packing machines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two influences on a firm's demand for a factor of production.
parts.answer: Any two of: the price (cost) of the factor, e.g. the wage rate; the productivity of the factor; the demand for the product it makes (derived demand); the price and productivity of other factors that could replace it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid influences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the firm should replace the workers with machines.
parts.answer: Depends on relative costs, productivity and the firm's market.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': machines work faster and longer without breaks, raising productivity; lower average cost in the long run; more consistent quality and hygiene; fewer labour problems such as strikes. Up to 3 marks for 'should not': high initial cost and maintenance; machines may break down and need skilled technicians; workers are cheap and flexible; if demand falls, idle machines still have to be paid for; loss of goodwill and redundancy costs. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a function of a central bank rather than a commercial bank?
A accepting deposits from households
B acting as the banker to the government
C lending money to small businesses
D providing loans to people buying houses
parts.answer: B acting as the banker to the government
parts.working: A central bank is the government's banker (it also issues the currency, is lender of last resort and conducts monetary policy). Accepting household deposits (A) and lending to firms (C) and house buyers (D) are functions of commercial banks.

practice.stem: In many countries, including Pakistan and Kenya, people pay shopkeepers and send money to relatives using balances held in mobile phone wallets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two functions of money.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: medium of exchange – money is accepted in payment for goods, avoiding the need for a double coincidence of wants in barter; unit of account/measure of value – prices of different goods can be compared in one unit; store of value – money can be saved and used later; standard for deferred payment – debts can be agreed now and repaid in future.
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark for the function, 1 mark for explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mobile-wallet balances can act as money.
parts.answer: They are generally acceptable to sellers as payment and have the characteristics of money: portable, divisible into small amounts and durable, so they can act as a medium of exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark: generally accepted as payment / medium of exchange. 1 mark: a relevant characteristic (portable, divisible, durable, hard to forge).

practice.stem: Commercial banks in a country raise the interest rate they pay on savings accounts from 8% to 11% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest earned in one year on savings of Rs 250 000 at the new rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the growth of commercial banking benefits an economy.
parts.answer: Benefits through saving, lending and payments, but there are risks.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for benefits: safe place for savings and interest for savers; loans to firms finance investment and growth; loans to households for housing/cars raise living standards; efficient payment systems help trade. Up to 3 marks for problems: banks aim for profit, so they may charge high interest or ignore small firms/poor households; excessive lending can cause debt problems, inflation or asset bubbles; bank failures can harm savers and the whole economy; banks may concentrate in cities. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. benefits depend on regulation by the central bank).

practice.stem:
A café sells meals at Rs 250 each. The table shows its total cost per day at different outputs.
Meals per day | Total cost (Rs)
0 | 8 000
50 | 13 000
100 | 17 000
150 | 22 500

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the café's fixed cost per day.
parts.working: B1: Rs 8 000 (total cost when output is zero).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average total cost per meal when 100 meals are sold.
parts.answer: Rs 170

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the café's profit when it sells 150 meals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why average fixed cost falls as output increases.
parts.answer: Fixed cost stays the same (Rs 8 000) whatever the output, so as more meals are produced it is spread over a larger number of units, so the fixed cost per meal falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: total fixed cost does not change with output. 1 mark: divided by more units, so AFC falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm has fixed costs of Rs 60 000. At an output of 3 000 units its average variable cost is Rs 25. What is its average total cost at this output?
A Rs 20
B Rs 25
C Rs 45
D Rs 85
parts.answer: C Rs 45
parts.working: Total cost = 60 000 + 25 × 3 000 = 135 000; average total cost = 135 000 ÷ 3 000 = Rs 45 (= AFC 20 + AVC 25). Rs 20 (A) is only average fixed cost and Rs 25 (B) only average variable cost.

practice.stem: A large food company says its main aim is to maximise profit. A social enterprise selling low-cost water filters says its main aim is to improve health in poor villages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives a firm might have other than profit maximisation.
parts.answer: Any two of: survival; growth / increasing sales; increasing market share; social welfare / helping the community; providing a good service; protecting the environment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a firm should always aim to maximise profit.
parts.answer: Profit is important, but other aims may be more suitable at times.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': rewards owners/shareholders for risk; provides funds for investment and growth; shows efficient use of resources; attracts finance. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': a new firm may aim to survive or grow first; cutting prices to gain market share may be better long term; social enterprises and public-sector firms aim at welfare; pursuing profit may harm reputation (pollution, poor treatment of workers); owners may want a comfortable life rather than maximum profit. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is most likely to cause a household to save more of its income?
A a fall in the household's income
B a rise in the interest rate paid on savings
C easier access to credit cards
D greater confidence that the household's jobs are secure
parts.answer: B a rise in the interest rate paid on savings
parts.working: A higher interest rate increases the reward for saving, so households tend to save more. Lower income (A) usually reduces saving; easy credit (C) encourages borrowing and spending; job security (D) reduces the need for precautionary saving.

practice.stem: A household in Lahore has a monthly disposable income of Rs 180 000. It spends Rs 153 000 a month and saves the rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the household's saving as a percentage of its disposable income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a high-income household usually saves a larger proportion of its income than a low-income household.
parts.answer: Low-income households must spend almost all their income on necessities such as food, rent and fuel, so little is left to save. High-income households can meet their needs with a smaller share of income, so they can save more; they also have better access to banks and saving schemes and may save for large future purchases or investments.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: The central bank of a country cuts its interest rate from 15% to 12%, and commercial banks reduce the interest they charge on loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a household might borrow.
parts.answer: Any two of: to buy a house; to buy expensive durable goods such as a car or motorcycle; to pay for education; to pay for a wedding or emergency; to start a small business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the fall in interest rates will cause households to borrow more.
parts.answer: Borrowing is likely to rise but depends on other influences.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'will': loans are cheaper, so repayments fall; more households can afford house or car loans; saving is less rewarding, so spending financed by credit rises. Up to 3 marks for 'may not': households worried about job security or a recession may not borrow; they may already have high debts; banks may not lend if they think borrowers are risky; a cut of 3 percentage points may be too small to change decisions; religious or cultural reasons may discourage interest-based borrowing. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a trade union.
parts.answer: An organisation of workers that acts on behalf of its members to protect and improve their pay and working conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: association/organisation of workers. 1 mark: aims to improve pay/conditions/job security of members.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that affect the strength of a trade union.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: the proportion of workers who are members – a high membership gives more bargaining power; the skills of members – skilled workers are hard to replace during a strike; the state of the economy – when unemployment is low, firms find it harder to replace workers; laws on strikes and union activity; the financial health of the employer; public support.
parts.working: For each of two factors: 1 mark for the factor, 1 mark for explaining how it affects bargaining power.

practice.stem: A teachers' union asks for an increase in its members' average monthly pay from Rs 90 000 to Rs 103 500. Prices in the country rose by 12% over the past year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage pay rise that the union is asking for.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a trade union is always beneficial for its members.
parts.answer: Usually beneficial, but not always.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'beneficial': collective bargaining wins higher pay (e.g. protecting real wages when prices rise 12%); better working conditions, safety and job security; legal advice and representation; training. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': members pay subscriptions; strikes mean lost pay; high wage rises may cause employers to cut jobs or replace workers with machines; a weak union may achieve little; members may disagree with the union's decisions. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a labour force of 60 million people, of whom 4.2 million are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A 7.0 %
B 7.5 %
C 6.5 %
D 70 %
parts.working: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 4.2 ÷ 60 × 100 = 7.0 %. B divides by the number employed (55.8 million), giving about 7.5 %, instead of by the whole labour force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define unemployment.
parts.answer: Being of working age, willing and able to work, actively seeking work, but without a job.
parts.working: 1 mark: willing and able to work/of working age; 1 mark: without a job but looking for one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify and explain two types of unemployment.
parts.answer: e.g. frictional – people between jobs; structural – mismatch caused by long-term decline of an industry
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming two types + 1 mark each for explanation: frictional (between jobs, searching); structural (decline of an industry/change in skills needed); cyclical (lack of demand in a recession); seasonal (demand varies with seasons, e.g. tourism, harvest).

practice.stem: In a country, the working-age population is 130 million. The labour force is 75 million, of whom 69 million are employed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of people unemployed.
parts.answer: 6 million
parts.working: B1 75 − 69 = 6 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the working-age population that is in the labour force. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two consequences of unemployment for the government.
parts.answer: Lower income tax revenue; higher spending on unemployment benefits/welfare
parts.working: 1 mark each for two consequences + 1 mark each for development: less tax revenue (income and indirect taxes); more spending on benefits; larger budget deficit/more borrowing; opportunity cost – less to spend on schools/hospitals; social problems such as crime raise costs; loss of votes/popularity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why automation in textile mills in Faisalabad could cause structural unemployment.
parts.answer: Machines replace workers; the displaced workers' skills no longer match the jobs available, so they stay unemployed for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark: machines replace labour/fewer workers needed; 1 mark: workers' skills do not match jobs elsewhere (occupational immobility); 1 mark: long-term unemployment linked to a change in the structure of the industry.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two government policies that could reduce this type of unemployment.
parts.answer: Retraining schemes to give workers new skills; subsidies/grants for firms that set up in the area or employ these workers
parts.working: 1 mark each for two policies + 1 mark each for explanation: retraining/vocational courses improve occupational mobility; relocation grants/housing help geographical mobility; subsidies to firms that hire; better job information centres; attracting new industries to the region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a rise in unemployment is always bad for an economy.
parts.answer: Usually harmful (lost output, lower incomes, lower tax revenue, social costs), but may be short-term frictional, can reduce inflationary pressure and may reflect structural change that raises productivity later.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for harm: output below potential/lost GDP; lower incomes and living standards; lower tax revenue and higher benefit spending; skills lost; poverty, crime, health problems. Up to 5 marks for why not always bad: frictional unemployment may be short and improve job matching; lower wage pressure may reduce inflation; labour available for new expanding industries; firms may become more efficient. Max 8; conclusion required for top band, e.g. depends on type and duration.

practice.stem:
Real GDP growth (%) and unemployment rate (%) for five countries in one year:
Country A: growth 6.1, unemployment 4.0
Country B: growth 3.5, unemployment 6.2
Country C: growth 1.2, unemployment 8.9
Country D: growth −0.8, unemployment 11.5
Country E: growth 4.0, unemployment 7.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest unemployment rate.
parts.answer: Country D (11.5 %)
parts.working: B1 Country D.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the relationship between economic growth and the unemployment rate shown in the table.
parts.answer: Generally an inverse relationship: higher growth, lower unemployment (A highest growth 6.1 %, lowest unemployment 4.0 %; D negative growth, highest unemployment). Exception: E has higher growth than B but higher unemployment, so other factors (e.g. structural unemployment, labour force growth) matter.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse/negative relationship; 1 mark: data comparison using two countries (A and D); 1 mark: reason – growth raises demand for goods and so for labour (derived demand); 1 mark: exception identified (E vs B); 1 mark: explanation of exception, e.g. growth driven by capital-intensive industries, fast-growing labour force, structural or frictional factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a progressive tax?
A a tax that takes a higher proportion of income as income rises
B a tax that takes the same proportion of income at all income levels
C a tax that takes the same amount from everyone
D a tax that takes a lower proportion of income as income rises
parts.answer: A a tax that takes a higher proportion of income as income rises
parts.working: A progressive tax has an average rate that rises with income. B is a proportional tax; D is a regressive tax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a direct tax and an indirect tax, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Direct tax is levied on income or wealth and paid directly to the government by the person taxed (e.g. income tax). Indirect tax is levied on spending on goods and services (e.g. sales tax/GST).
parts.working: 1 mark: direct tax on income/wealth; 1 mark: valid example (income tax, corporation tax, property tax); 1 mark: indirect tax on spending/goods and services; 1 mark: valid example (sales tax, GST/VAT, excise duty, customs duty).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why governments impose taxes.
parts.answer: To raise revenue for public spending; to redistribute income
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: raise revenue; redistribute income; discourage consumption of demerit goods/reduce external costs; protect domestic industries (tariffs); influence aggregate demand/manage the economy.

practice.stem:
A country's income tax bands are:
first $10 000 of income: 0 %
next $20 000 (from $10 001 to $30 000): 10 %
income above $30 000: 25 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by a person earning $50 000 a year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this person's average rate of tax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A person earning $20 000 pays $1 000 in tax. Explain whether this income tax system is progressive.
parts.answer: Yes: the average rate rises from 5 % at $20 000 to 14 % at $50 000.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate at $20 000 = 5 %; 1 mark: rising average rate with income, so progressive.

practice.stem: In one year, a government's revenue is $120 billion and its spending is $138 billion. The country's GDP is $450 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit.
parts.answer: $18 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the government could reduce the budget deficit.
parts.answer: Raise tax revenue (e.g. higher tax rates, wider tax base); cut government spending (e.g. on subsidies)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two ways + 1 mark each for explanation: increase tax rates; widen tax base/reduce tax evasion; cut current spending (subsidies, wages); delay capital projects; privatise state firms to raise revenue; encourage economic growth which raises tax revenue automatically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a cut in income tax rates will increase economic growth.
parts.answer: Could raise disposable income and spending, and improve incentives to work and invest; but extra income may be saved or spent on imports, supply may not respond if near capacity, and lower revenue may force cuts in public investment or more borrowing.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for why it may: higher disposable income → more consumption → higher aggregate demand → more output; stronger incentive to work/more hours; more saving available for investment; attracts skilled workers. Up to 5 marks for why it may not: income saved (low confidence); spending on imports; inflation if economy near full capacity; lower government revenue → less spending on infrastructure/education or bigger deficit; small effect if many workers earn below the tax threshold. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy can reduce unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: Higher government spending and/or lower taxes raise aggregate demand; firms sell more and need more workers (labour is a derived demand), reducing cyclical unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase spending/cut taxes; 1 mark: aggregate demand rises; 1 mark: firms raise output; 1 mark: demand for labour rises, cyclical unemployment falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why expansionary fiscal policy may fail to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: e.g. time lags in planning and spending; unemployment may be structural, so extra demand does not match workers' skills
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: time lags; structural/frictional unemployment not caused by low demand; extra income saved or spent on imports; government cannot afford more borrowing/debt; firms use spare capacity or machines rather than hiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define inflation.
parts.answer: A sustained rise in the general price level over a period of time.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise in general price level; 1 mark: sustained/over time (fall in value of money).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of inflation.
parts.answer: Demand-pull: aggregate demand rises faster than output. Cost-push: higher costs of production (wages, imported oil) passed on as higher prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: demand-pull (spending > output capacity); cost-push (higher wages, raw materials, energy, import costs after depreciation); increase in money supply; higher indirect taxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer price index has three categories. In the base year each category had an index of 100. One year later: food (weight 0.5) has an index of 112, transport (weight 0.3) 120 and other items (weight 0.2) 105. What is the rate of inflation?
A 13 %
B 12.3 %
C 37 %
D 11.3 %
parts.working: Weighted index = 0.5 × 112 + 0.3 × 120 + 0.2 × 105 = 56 + 36 + 21 = 113, so prices rose 13 %. B is the unweighted average (112.3), which ignores the weights.

practice.stem:
A country's consumer price index (CPI):
Year 1: 150
Year 2: 162
Year 3: 170.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A newspaper says 'prices fell in Year 3'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Inflation fell (disinflation) but was still positive, so prices continued to rise, only more slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark: index still rose/inflation still positive; 1 mark: rate of increase slowed – this is not deflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether deflation is harmful to an economy.
parts.answer: Harmful if caused by falling demand: consumers delay purchases, profits fall, unemployment rises, real debt burden rises. Less harmful if caused by lower costs/higher productivity: real incomes rise and exports become more competitive.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for harm: postponed spending lowers aggregate demand; firms cut output and jobs; real value of debts rises, so borrowers suffer and spending falls; falling profits reduce investment; difficult for central bank to cut interest rates further. Up to 5 marks for not harmful: 'good' deflation from lower costs/new technology; higher real incomes, especially for people on fixed incomes and savers; improved international competitiveness. Max 8; judgement on cause/size/length needed for top band.

practice.stem: A worker's monthly wage rises from Rs 40 000 to Rs 44 000 over a year in which inflation is 12 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's money (nominal) wage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's real wage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how inflation affects savers and borrowers.
parts.answer: Savers lose if inflation exceeds the interest rate, as the real value of savings falls; borrowers gain because the real value of their debts falls.
parts.working: Savers: 1 mark real value of savings falls, 1 mark if interest rate < inflation (negative real interest). Borrowers: 1 mark real value of debt falls, 1 mark repay with money worth less.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Economic growth is best measured by an increase in which of the following?
A real GDP
B nominal (money) GDP
C the size of the population
D the money supply
parts.answer: A real GDP
parts.working: Economic growth is an increase in real GDP, i.e. output adjusted for inflation. B can rise just because prices rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a recession.
parts.answer: A fall in real GDP for two consecutive quarters (six months or more).
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in real GDP/negative economic growth; 1 mark: for two consecutive quarters/six months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two consequences of a recession.
parts.answer: Rising unemployment as firms cut output; lower tax revenue and higher benefit spending for the government
parts.working: 1 mark each for two consequences + 1 mark each for explanation: unemployment rises; incomes and living standards fall; firms' profits fall and some close; government tax revenue falls/benefit spending rises; inflation usually falls; imports fall.

practice.stem: A country's real GDP rose from $380 billion to $395.2 billion in one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The population grew by 2.5 % in the same year. Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two causes of economic growth.
parts.answer: Investment in capital goods; improvements in education and training (human capital)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: more investment in machinery and infrastructure; better education/skills raise productivity; new technology; discovery of natural resources; more workers (e.g. immigration, higher participation); higher aggregate demand using spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether economic growth always benefits the people of a country.
parts.answer: Growth can raise incomes, jobs and tax revenue for public services, but may damage the environment, deplete resources, widen inequality, cause inflation or longer working hours, and benefits depend on population growth.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: higher real incomes and living standards; more jobs/lower unemployment; more tax revenue for schools and hospitals without raising tax rates; reduced poverty. Up to 5 marks for costs: pollution and climate damage; depletion of non-renewable resources; inequality – gains go to a few; inflation; stress/longer hours; GDP per head may not rise if population grows faster. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two monetary policy measures.
parts.answer: Changing interest rates; changing the money supply
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: interest rate changes; changes in the money supply; changes in the exchange rate (managed by the central bank).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a cut in interest rates can increase consumer spending.
parts.answer: Borrowing becomes cheaper so more people take loans for cars and homes; the reward for saving falls so people save less; existing borrowers with variable-rate loans pay less interest and have more disposable income.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowing cheaper; 1 mark: more spending on credit (e.g. cars, appliances); 1 mark: saving less attractive so more spent; 1 mark: lower repayments on existing loans raise disposable income.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank raises its interest rate. What is the most likely effect?
A consumers borrow and spend less
B firms increase investment
C the country's currency depreciates
D the rate of inflation rises
parts.answer: A consumers borrow and spend less
parts.working: Higher interest rates make loans more expensive and saving more rewarding, so consumer borrowing and spending fall. The currency usually appreciates (C wrong) as foreign savers are attracted, and investment falls (B wrong).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country's central bank raises its interest rate to reduce inflation. Discuss whether higher interest rates will reduce inflation.
parts.answer: Likely to reduce demand-pull inflation by cutting borrowing and spending and by appreciating the currency; less effective against cost-push inflation, if many people do not borrow from banks, if time lags are long, or if the higher rates cut investment and growth.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for why it may work: dearer loans → less consumption and investment → lower aggregate demand; more saving; currency appreciation lowers import prices; reduced expectations of inflation. Up to 5 marks for why it may not: inflation is cost-push (e.g. imported oil prices); many households use cash/informal credit; time lags; government spending financed by borrowing keeps demand high; side effects – unemployment, lower growth, higher cost of government debt. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a supply-side policy?
A investment in vocational training
B an increase in interest rates
C an increase in unemployment benefits
D an increase in import tariffs
parts.answer: A investment in vocational training
parts.working: Supply-side policies aim to raise the productive capacity of the economy; training raises labour productivity. B is monetary policy and D is protectionism.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how two supply-side policies could increase labour productivity.
parts.answer: Education and training raise workers' skills; tax incentives or subsidies for investment give workers better capital equipment
parts.working: 1 mark each for two policies + 1 mark each for explanation: education/training; better health care; subsidies/tax allowances for investment in machinery and technology; improved infrastructure (roads, power supply); deregulation/privatisation increasing competition and efficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why supply-side policies may take a long time to have an effect.
parts.answer: e.g. education and infrastructure projects take years to complete before output rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: long time to train workers/build infrastructure; 1 mark: so productive capacity increases only in the long run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the privatisation of a state-owned electricity company will improve its efficiency.
parts.answer: The profit motive and access to private finance may cut costs and improve service; but a private monopoly may raise prices, cut unprofitable rural supply and under-invest, so regulation and competition matter.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for improvement: profit motive encourages cost cutting and less waste; private investment funds new power plants; less political interference; competition if market opened. Up to 5 marks for why not: may become a private monopoly – higher prices, less output; may cut supply to unprofitable remote areas; job losses; regulation needed; efficiency depends on management not ownership. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT usually a macroeconomic aim of a government?
A maximising the profits of private firms
B low and stable inflation
C economic growth
D low unemployment
parts.answer: A maximising the profits of private firms
parts.working: The usual macroeconomic aims are economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices, balance of payments stability and redistribution of income. Profit maximisation is an objective of individual firms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two macroeconomic aims of a government, other than full employment and low inflation.
parts.answer: Economic growth; balance of payments stability
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: economic growth; balance of payments stability; redistribution of income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the aim of full employment may conflict with the aim of low inflation.
parts.answer: Policies that raise aggregate demand to cut unemployment push up demand for goods and labour; with fewer spare workers, wages and prices rise, causing demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark: policies to reduce unemployment raise aggregate demand; 1 mark: demand may exceed output capacity → demand-pull inflation; 1 mark: shortage of labour pushes up wages; 1 mark: firms pass on higher wage costs – cost-push inflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two roles of a government in a national economy.
parts.answer: e.g. as a producer of goods and services such as education and roads; as a regulator protecting consumers and the environment
parts.working: 1 mark each for two roles + 1 mark each for explanation: producer (public and merit goods); employer (civil servants, teachers); regulator (laws on competition, pollution, safety); redistributor of income (taxes and benefits); manager of the economy (fiscal, monetary, supply-side policies).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one international role of a government.
parts.answer: e.g. negotiating trade agreements with other countries
parts.working: B1 any one: member of international organisations (e.g. WTO); negotiating trade agreements; setting tariffs; giving or receiving aid; cooperating on environmental issues.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government wants to reduce the consumption of cigarettes, a demerit good. Which policy is most likely to achieve this?
A an indirect tax on cigarettes
B a subsidy to cigarette producers
C a reduction in the import duty on cigarettes
D removing the ban on smoking in public places
parts.answer: A an indirect tax on cigarettes
parts.working: An indirect tax raises producers' costs, shifts supply left and raises the price, so the quantity demanded falls. B, C and D would all raise consumption: B and C lower costs/prices (supply shifts right), and D removes a restriction on where people can smoke.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a subsidy.
parts.answer: A payment made by the government to producers (or consumers) to lower the cost of producing or buying a product.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment/grant from the government; 1 mark: to producers to reduce costs/lower price or encourage output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a city government might subsidise public bus services in Lahore.
parts.answer: e.g. to reduce traffic congestion and pollution (external costs); to make travel affordable for low-income workers
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 mark for development, any two of: lower fares encourage people to switch from cars, reducing congestion and air pollution (external costs); public transport has external benefits so would be under-consumed in a free market; helps low-income households reach jobs and schools; keeps bus routes running that would be unprofitable; reduces fuel imports.

practice.stem:
The table shows the weekly market for wheat flour in a city.
Price (Rs per kg): 80, 90, 100, 110, 120
Quantity demanded (thousand kg): 700, 650, 600, 550, 500
Quantity supplied (thousand kg): 300, 400, 480, 550, 610

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity of wheat flour.
parts.answer: Rs 110 per kg; 550 thousand kg per week
parts.working: B1 price Rs 110; B1 quantity 550 thousand kg (where quantity demanded = quantity supplied).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a maximum price of Rs 90 per kg. Calculate the shortage that results.
parts.answer: 250 thousand kg per week
parts.working: M1 at Rs 90: quantity demanded 650, quantity supplied 400; A1 650 − 400 = 250 thousand kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two possible consequences of this maximum price.
parts.answer: e.g. queues/shortages leading to rationing; a black (illegal) market at higher prices
parts.working: 1 mark for each consequence identified + 1 mark for each explanation, any two of: shortage so queues form/some consumers go without; rationing or first-come-first-served allocation needed; black market develops where flour is sold above the legal price; producers earn less so may cut output or quality in the long run; poorer households can buy flour more cheaply (if they can obtain it).

practice.stem: A government sets a minimum price for cotton of $1.60 per kg. The free-market equilibrium price is $1.40 per kg. At the minimum price, farmers supply 900 tonnes and buyers demand 650 tonnes (1 tonne = 1000 kg).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surplus of cotton at the minimum price.
parts.answer: 250 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government buys the whole surplus at the minimum price. Calculate the cost to the government.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether a minimum price is the best way for the government to help cotton farmers.
parts.answer: Balanced answer: guarantees farmers a higher, stable income, but creates a surplus, costs the government money, raises prices for textile firms and may encourage over-production; alternatives such as subsidies for better seeds or direct income support may be better.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for why it may help: higher and more certain income for farmers; reduces risk so farmers keep growing cotton; protects rural jobs. Up to 3 marks for why it may not: surplus must be bought and stored at a cost ($400 000) – opportunity cost of government spending; higher input price for textile mills reduces their competitiveness; encourages inefficient farmers to stay; alternatives (subsidy on inputs, training, direct cash support) may be cheaper. Max 5; a conclusion is needed for full marks.

practice.stem: A government places a specific (per-unit) tax of 30 cents on each can of sugary drink. Before the tax, the price was $1.00 and 2.0 million cans were sold each week. After the tax, the price is $1.20 and 1.7 million cans are sold each week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the government's weekly revenue from the tax.
parts.working: M1 tax per can × cans sold after tax = $0.30 × 1.7 million; A1 $510 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the tax per can that is paid by consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tax might not reduce the consumption of sugary drinks very much.
parts.answer: Demand for sugary drinks is price inelastic (e.g. they are habit-forming, a can takes a small share of income and consumers see few satisfactory substitutes), so the price rise causes a smaller percentage fall in quantity demanded.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand is price inelastic; up to 3 more marks for development: drinks are habit-forming; spending on a can is a small share of income; few substitutes that consumers see as close; tax only partly passed on to consumers (price rose by 20 cents, not 30); consumers may switch to other untaxed sugary foods, so total sugar intake changes little; here a 20 % price rise cut quantity by only 15 % (PED −0.75).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of chicken feed falls. State what happens to the supply curve of chicken meat.
parts.answer: It shifts to the right (supply increases).
parts.working: B1 shifts right/outwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, describing a demand and supply diagram, the effect of this change on the equilibrium price and quantity of chicken meat.
parts.answer: Supply curve shifts right; at the old price there is excess supply; price falls and quantity rises to a new equilibrium.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower costs of production so supply curve shifts from S1 to S2 (right); 1 mark: excess supply at original price; 1 mark: equilibrium price falls (P1 to P2); 1 mark: equilibrium quantity rises (Q1 to Q2), a movement along the demand curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define complementary goods.
parts.answer: Goods that are used together, so a change in the price of one changes the demand for the other in the opposite direction (joint demand).
parts.working: 1 mark: goods used together/joint demand; 1 mark: e.g. cars and petrol, or the inverse price–demand relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of a fall in the price of petrol on the demand for cars.
parts.answer: Running a car becomes cheaper, so demand for cars rises (curve shifts right).
parts.working: 1 mark: cars cheaper to run/more attractive; 1 mark: demand for cars increases, curve shifts right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other cause of an increase in the demand for cars.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in incomes
parts.working: Any one: higher incomes; cheaper car loans (lower interest rates); population growth; rise in price of public transport (substitute); advertising.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Floods in Sindh destroy part of the mango crop. Explain the effect on the market for mangoes.
parts.answer: Supply falls (curve shifts left), creating excess demand at the old price, so price rises and quantity bought and sold falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply decreases/curve shifts left; 1 mark: fewer mangoes available at each price; 1 mark: price rises; 1 mark: equilibrium quantity falls (contraction along demand curve).

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the same time, incomes in the country rise so the demand for mangoes increases. Explain why the equilibrium price of mangoes will definitely rise but the change in equilibrium quantity is uncertain.
parts.answer: Both a fall in supply and a rise in demand push price up; the fall in supply lowers quantity while the rise in demand raises it, so the net effect depends on which shift is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: both shifts raise price; 1 mark: supply shift reduces quantity, demand shift increases it; 1 mark: final quantity depends on relative size of the two shifts.

practice.stem:
The table shows the market for smartphones in a country.
Year 1: average price $250, quantity sold 4.0 million
Year 2: average price $220, quantity sold 4.8 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the average price of smartphones between the two years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify whether a shift in demand or a shift in supply best explains the change in price and quantity, and give one possible cause.
parts.answer: An increase (rightward shift) in supply, e.g. cheaper components or new technology lowering production costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply increased/shifted right; 1 mark: because price fell while quantity rose (a demand increase would raise price); 1 mark for a valid cause: lower cost of components, new technology, more firms entering, subsidy, lower import duty.

practice.stem: A medical report says that a high intake of sugar harms health. At the same time, the price of honey, a substitute for sugar, rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of each event on the demand for sugar.
parts.answer: Health report: tastes change, demand falls (shifts left). Rise in honey price: honey is a substitute so consumers switch to sugar, demand rises (shifts right).
parts.working: Health report: 1 mark demand curve shifts left, 1 mark consumers see sugar as harmful/tastes change. Honey: 1 mark demand for sugar shifts right, 1 mark sugar now relatively cheaper substitute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the equilibrium price of sugar will rise or fall.
parts.answer: It depends on which shift is larger: if the health effect is stronger, demand falls overall and price falls; if the substitution effect is stronger, price rises; if equal, price unchanged. Honey may be a weak substitute, so the health effect may dominate.
parts.working: 1 mark: net effect depends on relative size of shifts; 1 mark: larger fall → price falls; 1 mark: larger rise → price rises; 1 mark: judgement, e.g. honey is much more expensive/used differently so is a weak substitute; or supply unchanged so price follows net demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define price elasticity of demand.
parts.answer: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the product's price.
parts.working: 1 mark: responsiveness/sensitivity of quantity demanded; 1 mark: to a change in its own price (or the formula % change in Qd ÷ % change in price).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the demand for salt is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Few close substitutes; it takes a very small share of income; it is a necessity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: no close substitutes so consumers keep buying; small proportion of income so a price rise is hardly noticed; necessity used in cooking every day; bought in small amounts infrequently.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price of a product rises from $8 to $10. The quantity demanded falls from 500 units to 450 units. What is the price elasticity of demand?
A −0.4
B −2.5
C −0.1
D −4.0
parts.working: % change in quantity demanded = −50/500 = −10 %; % change in price = 2/8 = +25 %; PED = −10 ÷ 25 = −0.4. B inverts the formula (price change ÷ quantity change).

practice.stem: A bus company in Karachi raises its fare from Rs 50 to Rs 60. The number of passengers falls from 12 000 to 9 000 per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for bus travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the company's daily total revenue.
parts.answer: Falls by Rs 60 000 (from Rs 600 000 to Rs 540 000)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why your answer to (b) is consistent with your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Demand is price elastic (PED > 1 in size), so the percentage fall in passengers is greater than the percentage rise in fare and revenue falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand is elastic; 1 mark: %ΔQd larger than %ΔP so total revenue falls when price rises.

practice.stem: A cinema estimates that the price elasticity of demand is −0.6 for weekend tickets and −1.8 for weekday tickets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the quantity demanded of weekday tickets if the cinema cuts the weekday price by 10 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the cinema should cut the price of both weekday and weekend tickets.
parts.answer: Cut weekday prices (elastic: revenue rises) but not weekend prices (inelastic: revenue falls); consider costs, capacity, competitors and accuracy of estimates.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: weekday demand elastic, 10 % cut raises Qd by 18 % so total revenue rises; weekend demand inelastic, cut raises Qd by only 6 % so revenue falls; may consider raising weekend prices instead. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: extra viewers raise snack sales; limited seats at weekends; estimates may be wrong or change; rivals may react; costs per extra viewer. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define demand.
parts.answer: The willingness and ability to buy a product at a given price over a period of time.
parts.working: 1 mark: willingness and ability (effective demand); 1 mark: at a given price/in a given time period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a movement along a demand curve and a shift of a demand curve.
parts.answer: A movement (extension/contraction) is caused only by a change in the product's own price; a shift is caused by a change in a non-price factor such as income, tastes or the price of related goods.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement caused by change in own price; 1 mark: extension when price falls/contraction when price rises; 1 mark: shift caused by change in other (non-price) factors; 1 mark: example, e.g. rise in income shifts demand right.

practice.stem:
Three consumers make up the market for a snack bar. Their weekly demand is:
Price $2: Ali 10, Bina 6, Chen 8
Price $3: Ali 7, Bina 5, Chen 6
Price $4: Ali 5, Bina 3, Chen 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market quantity demanded at a price of $3.
parts.answer: 18 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the market quantity demanded when the price rises from $2 to $4. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two factors, other than price, that could shift the market demand curve for this snack to the right.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in consumers' incomes; a successful advertising campaign
parts.working: 1 mark each for two factors + 1 mark each for explanation, any two of: higher incomes (normal good); advertising/change in tastes; rise in price of a substitute; fall in price of a complement; more consumers (population growth).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two products for which demand is likely to rise as the population ages.
parts.answer: e.g. health care/medicines and retirement homes
parts.working: 1 mark each for two: medical services, medicines, care homes, mobility aids, pensions/financial advice, leisure travel for retired people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how an ageing population could change the pattern of demand in an economy such as Japan.
parts.answer: Demand shifts towards health care, care services and products for older people and away from goods for the young (schools, baby products); total spending may fall as more people live on pensions; firms and labour move between markets.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: demand curves for health/care products shift right raising price and output (2); demand for products for young people (toys, schooling, starter homes) shifts left (2); lower average incomes of retired people reduce demand for some luxury goods/raise saving behaviour (1); resources reallocated through the price mechanism, e.g. more workers become carers (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define external cost.
parts.answer: A cost of an economic activity that falls on third parties who are not involved in it and is not paid by the producer or consumer.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost to a third party; 1 mark: not paid for/not included in the price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two external costs that a new cement factory could create for a nearby village in Punjab.
parts.answer: e.g. dust pollution causing breathing illnesses; heavy lorries causing noise and damaging roads
parts.working: 1 mark each for two costs + 1 mark each for explanation: air/dust pollution harming health and raising medical bills; noise; damage to crops from dust reducing farm income; congestion and road damage from lorries; water use lowering wells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two characteristics of a public good.
parts.answer: Non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting. Non-rival: one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable + 1 mark explanation; 1 mark: non-rival + 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a market system might not provide street lighting.
parts.answer: Because of the free-rider problem, consumers would not pay, so private firms could not make a profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: free-rider problem/people can benefit without paying; 1 mark: firms cannot charge so no profit, so it is not provided (missing market).

practice.stem: A chemical plant has private costs of $12 million a year and causes external costs of $5 million a year. Its private benefits are $15 million a year and it creates external benefits of $1 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the social cost and the social benefit of the plant.
parts.answer: Social cost $17 million; social benefit $16 million
parts.working: B1 social cost = private cost + external cost = 12 + 5 = $17m; B1 social benefit = 15 + 1 = $16m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plant would operate in a free market even though this may be a market failure.
parts.answer: The owner compares only private benefit ($15m) with private cost ($12m) and makes a profit; but social cost ($17m) exceeds social benefit ($16m), so society is worse off and resources are misallocated.
parts.working: 1 mark: private benefit > private cost so profitable; 1 mark: external costs ignored by the firm; 1 mark: social cost > social benefit so over-production/inefficient allocation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest and explain one government policy that could correct this market failure.
parts.answer: e.g. a tax on pollution equal to the external cost
parts.working: 1 mark: policy (pollution tax, regulation/emission limits, tradable permits, fines); up to 2 marks explaining how it makes the firm pay for or reduce the external cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market economic system, what mainly decides which goods are produced?
A consumer demand working through the price mechanism
B government planning officials
C trade unions
D the central bank
parts.answer: A consumer demand working through the price mechanism
parts.working: In a market system resources are allocated by the price mechanism: firms produce what consumers are willing and able to buy at a profit. B describes a planned economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a market economic system is better than a mixed economic system for a developing economy.
parts.answer: Balanced: market system gives incentives, choice and efficiency; but may under-provide public and merit goods, ignore external costs and create inequality, which a mixed system can address – though government failure is possible.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the market system: profit motive encourages efficiency and innovation; wide consumer choice; resources respond quickly to price signals; no costly bureaucracy. Up to 4 marks for the mixed system: government provides public goods (roads, street lights) and merit goods (education, health); corrects external costs; reduces inequality through taxes and benefits; protects consumers from monopolies. Evaluation (needed for top marks): depends on government efficiency/corruption, level of development, size of markets. Max 8.

practice.stem:
The table shows the daily market for notebooks in a town.
Price (Rs): 40, 50, 60, 70, 80
Quantity demanded: 900, 800, 700, 600, 500
Quantity supplied: 300, 500, 700, 900, 1100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the equilibrium price.
parts.answer: Rs 60
parts.working: B1 Rs 60 (quantity demanded = quantity supplied = 700).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the excess demand at a price of Rs 50.
parts.answer: 300 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the market would move to equilibrium if the price were Rs 50.
parts.answer: Shortage → consumers compete/sellers raise price → quantity supplied extends, quantity demanded contracts until Rs 60.
parts.working: 1 mark: shortage/excess demand at Rs 50; 1 mark: price is bid up; 1 mark: Qs rises and Qd falls until they are equal at Rs 60 (700 units).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At a price of $6, the quantity demanded of a product is 300 units and the quantity supplied is 500 units. What is the situation in this market?
A excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to fall
B excess demand of 200 units; the price will tend to rise
C excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to rise
D the market is in equilibrium
parts.answer: A excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to fall
parts.working: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 500 − 300 = 200, so there is a surplus; sellers cut prices to clear stocks. B confuses surplus with shortage.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a macroeconomic issue?
A the national unemployment rate
B the price of rice in one city market
C the wages of nurses at one hospital
D the output of a single car manufacturer
parts.answer: A the national unemployment rate
parts.working: Macroeconomics studies the whole economy, e.g. national unemployment, inflation, growth. B, C and D concern individual markets or decision makers, which is microeconomics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between microeconomics and macroeconomics.
parts.answer: Microeconomics studies individual markets and decision makers; macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole.
parts.working: 1 mark: micro – individual consumers, workers, firms or markets; 1 mark: macro – whole economy, e.g. inflation, unemployment, economic growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify three decision makers studied in microeconomics and give an example of a decision each makes.
parts.answer: e.g. households/consumers – what to buy; workers – which job to take; firms – what and how much to produce
parts.working: 1 mark each for three decision makers with a matching decision: consumers/households (spending, saving), workers (occupation, hours), firms/producers (output, prices, methods), government (as a decision maker in a market, e.g. setting a tax on one product).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would cause a movement along the supply curve of wheat rather than a shift of the curve?
A a rise in the price of wheat
B a subsidy paid to wheat farmers
C the introduction of higher-yield seeds
D a drought
parts.answer: A a rise in the price of wheat
parts.working: Only a change in the product's own price causes a movement (extension or contraction) along the supply curve. B, C and D change conditions of supply and shift the curve.

practice.stem: A farm's weekly supply of dates is 100 tonnes at $10 per kg, 200 tonnes at $20 per kg and 300 tonnes at $30 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: New technology increases the quantity supplied by 25 % at every price. Calculate the new quantity supplied at $20 per kg.
parts.answer: 250 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Farm workers' wages rise at the same time as the government introduces a subsidy for date farmers. Analyse the possible effect on the supply of dates.
parts.answer: Higher wages raise costs and shift supply left; the subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right; the overall effect depends on the relative size of the two changes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: higher wages raise costs of production, supply shifts left/less supplied at each price. Up to 2 marks: subsidy reduces costs/is extra revenue, supply shifts right. Up to 2 marks: net effect depends on which is larger; with demand unchanged, price falls if supply rises overall and rises if supply falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price of a product rises from $20 to $25 and the quantity supplied rises from 400 to 460 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
A 0.6
B 1.67
C 0.15
D 6.0
parts.working: % change in Qs = 60/400 = 15 %; % change in price = 5/20 = 25 %; PES = 15 ÷ 25 = 0.6 (inelastic). B inverts the formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of fresh tomatoes is price inelastic in the short run.
parts.answer: Tomatoes take months to grow so output cannot be increased quickly; they are perishable so stocks cannot be stored and released when the price rises.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: time needed to grow crops; perishable – no stocks; land and other resources already committed; farmers may lack spare capacity/greenhouses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the building of cold-storage warehouses could change the price elasticity of supply of tomatoes.
parts.answer: PES becomes more elastic because tomatoes can be stored and supplied to the market when prices rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply more elastic; 1 mark: stocks can be held and released quickly in response to price changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a protectionist measure?
A an import quota
B a free trade agreement
C the removal of a tariff
D a fall in international shipping costs
parts.answer: A an import quota
parts.working: A quota is a physical limit on the quantity of imports, so it protects domestic producers. B and C reduce trade barriers; D is a cause of globalisation, not a policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define globalisation.
parts.answer: The process by which the world's economies become more closely connected through trade, investment, movement of people and information.
parts.working: 1 mark: increasing integration/interdependence of economies; 1 mark: through trade, capital flows, MNCs, migration or technology.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of globalisation.
parts.answer: Improvements in transport (containers, air freight) lowered costs of trade; the internet and mobile communications make it easier to do business across borders
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: cheaper/faster transport; better communications/internet; reduced trade barriers and trade agreements; growth of MNCs; more freedom of capital movements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a government may protect its domestic industries.
parts.answer: To protect infant industries until they can compete; to protect jobs in domestic industries
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: infant industry argument; protect employment; prevent dumping; protect strategic industries (food, defence); reduce a current account deficit; raise tariff revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one method of protection other than a tariff.
parts.answer: e.g. a quota
parts.working: B1 any one: quota; embargo; subsidy to domestic producers; strict product standards/regulations; exchange controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country imposes an ad valorem tariff of 20 % on imported mobile phones. A phone has an import price of $150 before the tariff. If the whole tariff is passed on, what is the price after the tariff?
A $180
B $170
C $30
D $150
parts.working: 20 % of $150 = $30, so the price becomes $150 + $30 = $180. C is only the amount of the tariff.

practice.stem: Before a tariff, the world price of steel is $600 per tonne. A country demands 10 million tonnes a year and domestic firms supply 4 million tonnes, so 6 million tonnes are imported. The government imposes a tariff of $100 per tonne. Domestic supply rises to 5 million tonnes and domestic demand falls to 9 million tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity of steel imported after the tariff.
parts.answer: 4 million tonnes
parts.working: B1 9 − 5 = 4 million tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the government's revenue from the tariff.
parts.answer: $400 million
parts.working: M1 4 million × $100; A1 $400 million.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of the tariff for the country.
parts.answer: Steel users pay higher prices, raising costs for construction and car firms; other countries may retaliate with tariffs on the country's exports
parts.working: 1 mark each for two disadvantages + 1 mark each for explanation: higher prices for consumers/firms using steel; less choice; protected domestic firms may become inefficient; retaliation reduces exports; resources move to less efficient domestic producers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a multinational company (MNC).
parts.answer: A firm that has its headquarters in one country and production or operations in more than one country.
parts.working: 1 mark: firm operating/producing in more than one country; 1 mark: headquarters in one (home) country.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A foreign car manufacturer opens a factory in Pakistan. Explain two benefits to Pakistan.
parts.answer: Creates jobs and incomes; brings new technology and skills; may increase exports and tax revenue
