parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits + 1 mark each for explanation: employment and higher incomes; training and transfer of technology/management skills; tax revenue (corporation tax); exports improve the current account; more choice for consumers; local suppliers (parts makers) gain orders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define dumping.
parts.answer: Selling a product in a foreign market at a price below its cost of production (or below the price in the home market).
parts.working: 1 mark: selling exports abroad; 1 mark: at below cost/below home-market price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a government might respond to dumping by imposing a tariff.
parts.answer: Dumped imports undercut domestic firms, threatening output and jobs; a tariff raises the import price to a fair level so domestic firms can compete.
parts.working: 1 mark: dumped goods unfairly cheap; 1 mark: domestic firms lose sales/close, jobs lost; 1 mark: tariff raises price of imports and restores competition (anti-dumping duty).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a country should remove all its barriers to trade.
parts.answer: Free trade gives lower prices, more choice, competition and export opportunities through specialisation; but infant and strategic industries may need protection, jobs may be lost, dumping may occur and the country may become over-dependent on imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for removing barriers: lower prices/more choice for consumers; cheaper imported raw materials for firms; competition improves efficiency; specialisation raises world output; other countries more likely to lower their barriers. Up to 5 marks against: infant industries cannot compete; structural unemployment in declining industries; dumping; loss of tariff revenue; strategic industries (food, energy) at risk; current account deficit. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.stem: After joining a regional free trade area, a country's exports rose from $25 billion to $31 billion a year and its imports rose from $30 billion to $39 billion a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the country's exports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the country's imports.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Analyse why joining the free trade area might increase the country's imports by more than its exports.
parts.answer: Removing its own tariffs makes imports cheaper so demand rises; partner countries' firms may be more efficient; domestic firms may lack the capacity or quality to expand exports quickly; higher incomes also raise demand for imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: tariffs on imports removed, lowering import prices; 1 mark: consumers/firms switch from domestic goods to cheaper imports; 1 mark: domestic exporters face strong competition/slow to raise capacity or quality; 1 mark: other reason, e.g. imported capital goods needed by exporters, rising incomes, partners already had low tariffs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a quota and an embargo.
parts.answer: A quota limits the quantity of a product that can be imported; an embargo is a complete ban on trade in a product or with a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: quota – limit on quantity; 1 mark: embargo – total ban.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether a quota on imported cars will protect jobs in a country's car industry.
parts.answer: Restricting imports shifts demand to domestic producers, protecting jobs in the short run; but higher car prices reduce total sales, protected firms may stay inefficient, retaliation can cut exports and jobs, and car-dealing and service jobs linked to imports may be lost.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for protection: fewer imports, consumers buy domestic cars; domestic output and employment rise/are maintained; time for industry to become competitive. Up to 4 marks against: car prices rise so fewer cars sold overall; lack of competition → inefficiency, jobs at risk later; retaliation hurts exporters; jobs lost in import/sales businesses; domestic firms may use imported parts or automate. Max 6; judgement needed for top marks.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is recorded as a credit (inflow) in the trade in services section of a country's current account?
A spending by foreign tourists visiting the country
B imports of machinery
C interest paid to foreign banks
D spending by the country's residents on holidays abroad
parts.answer: A spending by foreign tourists visiting the country
parts.working: Foreign tourists' spending is an export of services, so it is a credit. B is a debit in trade in goods; C is a primary income debit; D is an import of services (debit).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four components of the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: Trade in goods; trade in services; primary income; secondary income
parts.working: 1 mark for any two; 2 marks for all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a current account deficit.
parts.answer: When the value of money flowing out of the country on the current account (imports of goods and services, income paid abroad) is greater than the value flowing in.
parts.working: 1 mark: debits/outflows exceed credits/inflows; 1 mark: on trade in goods and services plus primary and secondary income.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each item, state whether it is recorded in primary income or secondary income, and whether it is a credit or a debit for Pakistan:
(i) profits sent home by a foreign-owned company operating in Pakistan
(ii) money sent home by Pakistani workers in the Gulf
(iii) aid given by Pakistan's government to a country hit by an earthquake
(iv) interest received by Pakistani residents on savings held abroad
parts.answer: (i) primary income, debit; (ii) secondary income, credit; (iii) secondary income, debit; (iv) primary income, credit
parts.working: 1 mark for each item correctly classified (both section and credit/debit).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's current account shows (in $ billion): trade in goods −12, trade in services +4, primary income −3, secondary income +9. What is the current account balance?
A −$2 billion
B −$8 billion
C +$2 billion
D −$11 billion
parts.answer: A −$2 billion
parts.working: Current account = −12 + 4 − 3 + 9 = −$2 bn. B is only the balance of trade in goods and services (−12 + 4); D leaves out secondary income.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem:
Current account data for a country in one year ($ billion):
exports of goods 28; imports of goods 45
exports of services 7; imports of services 6
primary income credits 1; primary income debits 5
secondary income (net, mainly workers' remittances) +30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade in goods.
parts.answer: −$17 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance.
parts.answer: +$10 billion (surplus)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why workers' remittances are important for this country's current account.
parts.answer: Remittances (secondary income) of $30 bn more than offset the large deficit on trade in goods, turning the current account into a surplus and providing foreign currency to pay for imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: remittances recorded as secondary income credit; 1 mark: they cover the trade in goods deficit (30 > 17)/without them the current account would be in deficit (−$20 bn); 1 mark: provide foreign currency/support the exchange rate/raise household incomes.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of a current account deficit.
parts.answer: High domestic incomes raise spending on imports; high inflation or an appreciated currency makes exports uncompetitive
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: rising incomes → more imports; high relative inflation → exports dearer; exchange rate appreciation; low productivity/poor quality of exports; dependence on imported fuel or capital goods; large profit outflows to foreign firms (primary income).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one possible consequence of a long-term current account deficit.
parts.answer: e.g. pressure for the currency to depreciate, raising import prices and inflation
parts.working: 1 mark for consequence + 1 mark for explanation: currency depreciation/reserves fall; borrowing from abroad and growing foreign debt; loss of jobs in industries competing with imports; lower aggregate demand.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a current account deficit is always a problem for a country.
parts.answer: It can be a problem if long-lasting, financed by debt, or caused by uncompetitive industries; but it may be short-term, reflect imports of capital goods that raise future output, or be offset by financial inflows, and consumers gain from more imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for problem: debt and interest payments; reserves run down; downward pressure on currency → imported inflation; lost output and jobs; sign of uncompetitive industries. Up to 5 marks for not always: short-term or small relative to GDP; imports of machinery boost future growth and exports; financed by FDI; higher living standards from imported goods; may correct automatically under floating exchange rate. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a contractionary (deflationary) fiscal policy could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Higher taxes or lower government spending reduce disposable income and aggregate demand, so spending on imports falls; lower inflation also makes exports more competitive and firms may sell more abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark: raise taxes/cut government spending; 1 mark: lower disposable income/aggregate demand; 1 mark: less spending on imports; 1 mark: reduced inflationary pressure improves price competitiveness of exports/domestic firms seek export markets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of using this policy to reduce the deficit.
parts.answer: It reduces spending on domestic goods too, causing lower economic growth and higher unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (lower growth, unemployment, cuts to public services, unpopular); 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem: A country has GDP of $360 billion and a current account deficit of $14.4 billion. Its exports of goods are $40 billion and its imports of goods are $52 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The value of exports of goods rises by 10 % while imports of goods are unchanged. Calculate the new balance of trade in goods.
parts.answer: −$8 billion
parts.working: M1 new exports 40 × 1.1 = $44 bn; A1 44 − 52 = −$8 bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a country's export revenue might fall even though the volume of its exports rises.
parts.answer: If world prices of its exports fall by a larger percentage than the rise in volume, revenue (price × quantity) falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: export prices fall (e.g. commodity prices or depreciation in foreign-currency terms); 1 mark: price fall proportionally larger than volume rise, so price × quantity falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's currency appreciates against other currencies. What is the most likely effect?
A its exports become more expensive for foreign buyers
B its imports become more expensive for domestic buyers
C foreign tourists find it cheaper to visit the country
D its exports become more price competitive
parts.answer: A its exports become more expensive for foreign buyers
parts.working: After an appreciation each unit of foreign currency buys less of the domestic currency, so exports cost more in foreign currency. Imports become cheaper (B wrong) and exports less competitive (D wrong).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an exchange rate.
parts.answer: The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
parts.working: 1 mark: price/value of a currency; 1 mark: expressed in terms of another currency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of a depreciation of a currency in a floating exchange rate system.
parts.answer: A fall in demand for the currency, e.g. because exports fall; a rise in supply of the currency, e.g. because imports rise or interest rates are cut and savers move money abroad
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation (via demand/supply of the currency): fall in exports/foreign demand; rise in imports; lower interest rates; higher relative inflation; fall in foreign direct investment; speculation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The exchange rate of a country's currency, the rupee, changes from Rs 280 = $1 to Rs 300 = $1. An imported machine part costs $50. Which statement is correct?
A the rupee has depreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
B the rupee has appreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
C the rupee has depreciated and the part still costs Rs 14 000
D the rupee has appreciated and the part now costs Rs 13 000
parts.answer: A the rupee has depreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
parts.working: More rupees are needed to buy $1, so the rupee has depreciated. Cost = 50 × 300 = Rs 15 000 (up from 50 × 280 = Rs 14 000). B gets the price right but the direction wrong.

practice.stem: A machine made in Germany is priced at €20 000. The exchange rate changes from €1 = $1.10 to €1 = $1.25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the machine in US dollars before and after the change in the exchange rate.
parts.answer: $22 000 before; $25 000 after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the dollar price of the machine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of this exchange rate change on the quantity of European machinery bought by US firms.
parts.answer: The machines are dearer in dollars, so US firms buy fewer (or switch to other suppliers), depending on price elasticity of demand.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher dollar price; 1 mark: quantity demanded falls/switch to US or other suppliers (more so if demand is elastic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate system and a fixed exchange rate system.
parts.answer: Floating: the rate is set by market demand for and supply of the currency. Fixed: the government or central bank sets the rate at a chosen level and maintains it.
parts.working: 1 mark: floating determined by market forces; 1 mark: fixed set and maintained by the government/central bank (by buying or selling currency).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of a fixed exchange rate for a country.
parts.answer: Certainty for exporters and importers, encouraging trade and investment; discipline to keep inflation low
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages + 1 mark each for explanation: certainty/less risk for traders and foreign investors; easier planning of prices and costs; prevents speculation; forces government to control inflation to stay competitive; stable import prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a depreciation of its currency will benefit an economy.
parts.answer: Exports become cheaper and imports dearer, which may raise output, jobs and improve the current account; but imported raw materials and fuel cost more, causing cost-push inflation, real incomes fall, foreign-currency debts rise, and benefits depend on price elasticity of demand for exports and imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: exports cheaper in foreign currency → more sold; imports dearer → consumers switch to domestic products; higher aggregate demand, output and employment; current account improves; more tourism. Up to 5 marks for costs: imported inflation (fuel, raw materials); lower living standards; foreign debts more expensive to repay; little benefit if demand for exports/imports is price inelastic or other countries retaliate. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.stem: A hotel in Hunza charges Rs 18 000 per night. The exchange rate changes from 1 Malaysian ringgit (RM) = Rs 60 to RM 1 = Rs 66.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per night of the hotel, in ringgit, before and after the exchange rate change. Give the second answer to the nearest ringgit.
parts.answer: RM 300 before; RM 273 after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of this exchange rate change on tourism to Pakistan and on Pakistan's current account.
parts.answer: Holidays in Pakistan become cheaper for Malaysian tourists, so more visit; tourist spending is an export of services, so the trade in services balance and current account improve (if demand is price elastic).
parts.working: 1 mark: rupee has depreciated against the ringgit/stay cheaper in ringgit; 1 mark: more foreign tourists; 1 mark: tourism spending is a services export/credit; 1 mark: current account improves, depending on elasticity or other changes (e.g. Pakistani travel to Malaysia becomes dearer).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is an advantage to a country of specialising in the products it can make most efficiently and trading with other countries?
A it can achieve a higher total output from its resources
B it becomes less dependent on other countries
C it develops a wider variety of domestic industries
D it avoids all transport costs
parts.answer: A it can achieve a higher total output from its resources
parts.working: Specialisation allows resources to be used where they are most productive, increasing output; the country trades for other goods. B and C are the opposite – specialisation increases dependence and narrows the range of domestic industries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specialisation at a national level.
parts.answer: When a country concentrates on producing the goods and services it is best at producing (and trades for others).
parts.working: 1 mark: country concentrates on a narrow range of products; 1 mark: those it produces most efficiently/trades for the rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages for a country of specialising in a narrow range of products.
parts.answer: If world demand or prices for its product fall, incomes and jobs fall sharply; it becomes dependent on imports of other goods, which may be disrupted
parts.working: 1 mark each for two disadvantages + 1 mark each for explanation: risk from fall in world demand/price; structural unemployment if the industry declines; dependence on imports (supply disruption, war); depletion of resources; competition from new low-cost producers.

practice.stem: Garments make up 82 % of the exports of a South Asian country whose total exports are worth $55 billion a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the country's garment exports.
parts.answer: $45.1 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to the country of specialising in garment production.
parts.answer: Economies of scale lower average costs, making garments competitive; large export earnings and employment, especially for women workers
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits + 1 mark each for explanation: economies of scale; workers become skilled/productive; export revenue/foreign currency; employment and income; attracts foreign investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk of this degree of specialisation.
parts.answer: Exports depend on one industry, so a fall in world demand or a rise in competition from lower-cost countries would cut export earnings and jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk identified (fall in world demand, new competitors, trade barriers abroad, rising wages); 1 mark: explanation of effect on export earnings/jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether consumers benefit when their country specialises and trades freely with other countries.
parts.answer: Consumers gain from lower prices, wider choice and better quality through competition and economies of scale; but may lose if jobs and incomes fall in declining industries, if supply is disrupted, if quality or safety standards are lower, or if foreign firms gain monopoly power.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: lower prices from efficient production/economies of scale; wider choice including goods not produced at home; competition raises quality; higher incomes from export industries. Up to 5 marks against: consumers are also workers – job losses in industries facing imports; vulnerability to supply disruptions and price shocks; unsafe imports; dumping may eventually reduce competition; depreciation may make imports expensive. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.
